newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zedillo says Mexico to 'draw the line' against U.S..
newsitem.headline: Zedillo says Mexico to 'draw the line' against U.S..

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo lashed out on Friday against a U.S. congressional vote against his country's record in the war on drugs, and said it was time for the United States to stop meddling in Mexican affairs.
Zedillo said the House of Representatives vote on Thursday to overturn President Bill Clinton's "certification" two weeks ago of Mexico as a trustworthy ally in the fight against drugs went too far.
"This is where we draw the line," Zedillo told Mexican reporters in Osaka during a visit to Japan. "Our sovereignty and dignity as a nation are not negotiable," he said.

The resolution by the House of Representatives would "decertify" Mexico in 90 days unless Clinton's reported substantial progress by Mexico in the anti-drug war. The president is expected to veto the measure.
The measure softens the blow to Mexico by waiving the economic sanctions normally involved in "decertification."

But it requires the Mexican government to authorize U.S. drug enforcement agents to carry guns in Mexico, take steps to wipe out high-level corruption and promise to extradite captured drug lords to the United States -- conditions that are politically impossible for Zedillo to meet.
"Mexico will not accept conditions or pressures of any kind," said Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria, accompanying Zedillo in Japan.
Zedillo's comments, his harshest so far in the controversy over certification, punctuated a chorus of protests by Mexican congressmen, government officials and everyday citizens.
"Hard-liners win the first round," said the influential daily Reforma. The pro-government Uno Mas Uno rejected the threat to Mexico's national sovereignty in an editorial.
Even the College of Civil Engineers took out a newspaper advertisement on Friday in support of Zedillo.
Others lambasted what they saw as a hypocritical United States judging other nations while Americans continue to provide the world's most lucrative drug market.

President Clinton is expected to block the House measure, which passed by a vote of 251-175, short of the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto. Morever, there is less support for publicly chastising Mexico in the U.S. Senate, which also will take up the issue.
Few Mexicans are willing to admit that cocaine barons have infiltrated the highest ranks of the Mexican government.
The country's top anti-drug official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, was arrested last month on charges he was on the payroll of the leader of the powerful Juarez cartel.
In Houston, witnesses in a court case against a former deputy attorney general have testified how drug money was funneled to government authorities in exchange for protection.
